title: Marks by the River
passage:
Ken's grandfather lived near a river that ran through a farming town. When Ken was younger, he thought the river was simply a place where people fished, walked, or watched birds. During one summer visit, however, his grandfather showed him something Ken had never noticed before: small marks painted on several bridges and walls near the water. His grandfather explained that the marks showed how high the water had risen during past floods. Some were low, but one was far above Ken's head. The river looked calm that day, so it was difficult for him to imagine water reaching so high. The next morning, they walked along the river again. This time, Ken looked for signs of flood protection. He saw wide open spaces beside the river, strong walls, and paths that could also be used by emergency vehicles. His grandfather explained that some fields near the river were designed to hold extra water during heavy rain. A town could not stop every natural disaster, he said, but it could prepare. Ken became interested and asked why the old flood marks had not been removed. His grandfather answered that the marks were part of the town's memory. New technology could warn people about dangerous weather, but old signs could also teach important lessons. If people forgot what had happened before, they might believe that a calm river could never become dangerous. When Ken returned home, he made a short presentation for his class. He used photos of the flood marks and explained what he had learned. One classmate said there was a similar mark near her home, but she had never known what it meant. Another student decided to ask his family about past disasters in their area. Ken's teacher then asked the class to walk around their own neighborhoods and look for objects connected with safety. Students found evacuation signs, raised storage areas, and old maps showing places where water had once collected. Ken had expected his summer visit to be quiet. Instead, it changed the way he saw familiar places. He learned that a town can carry its history in ordinary objects. A line on a wall or an old sign may look unimportant, but it can help people understand risks and make better choices in the future.

After his presentation, Ken's class made a small safety map for the school entrance. They marked where rainwater gathered, where bicycles crossed, and where emergency information was posted. The activity showed Ken that remembering past danger is most useful when it leads to practical preparation in the present.
translation:
健の祖父は、農村を流れる川の近くに住んでいました。幼いころの健にとって、川は釣りをしたり歩いたり鳥を見たりする場所にすぎませんでした。ところが夏に訪れたとき、祖父は橋や川沿いの壁に残る小さな印を見せました。それは過去の洪水で水がどこまで上がったかを示す印でした。中には健の頭よりはるかに高い位置にあるものもあり、穏やかな川からは想像できませんでした。翌朝、今度は洪水への備えを意識して歩くと、広い空き地、丈夫な壁、緊急車両も使える道などが見えてきました。川沿いの一部の土地は大雨のときに余分な水を受け止める役割もあると祖父は説明します。自然災害を完全に止めることはできなくても、備えることはできます。古い洪水の印を消さないのは、それが町の記憶だからでした。新しい技術による警報だけでなく、過去の痕跡も大切な教訓になります。帰宅後、健は写真を使ってクラスで発表しました。すると、家の近くにも似た印があるという生徒や、家族に昔の災害について聞いてみようという生徒が現れました。先生はさらに、自分の地域で安全に関係するものを探す課題を出しました。避難標識、高い位置の保管場所、昔水がたまった場所を示す地図などが見つかりました。健は、町の歴史は特別な資料館だけでなく、壁の線や古い看板のような普通のものにも残っていると学びました。それらは将来の危険を理解し、よりよい判断をする助けになるのです。

発表後、健のクラスは学校入口周辺の簡単な安全地図も作りました。雨水がたまる場所、自転車が横切る場所、緊急情報の掲示場所などを記しました。過去の危険を覚えることは、現在の具体的な備えにつながってこそ役立つのだと健は理解しました。
